overview: Reduced-form credit modeling gives up on explaining *why* a firm defaults and simply asks *when*, treating default as the first jump of a Poisson process with intensity λ. That surrender buys tractability: survival probabilities become exponentials, both CDS legs become survival-weighted sums, and the market spread itself calibrates λ through the credit triangle λ ≈ s/(1−R). The deep habit this model teaches is reading spreads as probabilities: 100bp with 40% recovery is the market whispering 'about 1.7% hazard per year'.
formula_latex: \lambda \approx \frac{s}{1-R}, \quad Q(t) = e^{-\lambda t}, \quad V = N\Big[(1{-}R)\sum_i DF_i\,\Delta Q_i \; - \; s_c \sum_i \tau_i DF_i Q_i\Big]

variables.name: Hazard rate
variables.why_it_matters: The instantaneous default intensity — the model's only free parameter, implied from the market spread. Conditional on surviving to t, the chance of defaulting in the next instant is λ·dt.

variables.name: Survival probability
variables.why_it_matters: The credit analogue of a discount factor. Premium payments are weighted by it (paid only while alive); protection payments by its decrements (paid exactly when it drops).

variables.name: Recovery rate
variables.why_it_matters: What creditors salvage in default. It enters twice with opposite signs — scaling the loss (1−R) down and the implied hazard up — so its net effect on a par CDS is famously muted, and on off-market positions subtle.

variables.name: Par spread
variables.why_it_matters: Protection leg divided by risky annuity: the running premium making the contract free to enter. The number actually quoted on credit screens.

assumptions: Default arrives as a surprise (Poisson jump) — no slow visible deterioration, no causal story.
Constant hazard rate: a flat credit curve. Real term structures of spread require piecewise λ(t).
Recovery is a known constant fraction, paid at default.
Interest rates and default are independent (discounting and survival factorize).
Premium accrual-on-default is ignored and defaults settle mid-period — small, standard educational simplifications.
limitations: Flat λ cannot fit an upward or inverted CDS curve — the whole term structure of credit is compressed to one number.
Recovery uncertainty is real (2008 settled some names near 10 cents) but modeled as a constant.
Independence of rates and credit fails exactly in crises, when both move together (wrong-way risk).
Says nothing about correlated defaults — portfolio credit (CDOs, indices) needs copulas or factor models on top.
when_to_use: Single-name CDS valuation, converting spreads into implied default probabilities, marking existing positions to the current spread, and CS01/recovery risk.
when_not_to_use: Multi-name correlation products, deeply distressed names (where recovery and timing dominate), or anywhere the credit term structure's shape carries the trade.
industry_usage: The industry's baseline: ISDA's standard CDS model is precisely a piecewise-flat hazard framework, making this the flat-curve special case of what every credit desk runs.
computational_complexity: O(n) in premium periods; calibration here is a closed-form triangle rather than a bootstrap.
